Issued at 341 AM EST Tue Nov 10 2026

Now through Tuesday Night...

Surface high pressure and a quasi-zonal flow pattern with a 
northwesterly component at the upper levels presides over the region 
this morning. Clear skies and calm winds have again helped result in 
decent radiational cooling, with temperatures in the mid 30 to low 
40s expected by daybreak. Dry and mild conditions are expected on 
Tuesday, with highs in the upper 60s/low 70s. Weak shortwave energy 
over the Red River Valley will pass by just off to our south, but 
with limited moisture in place no precipitation is anticipated with 
this wave even if the track shifted north. For Tuesday night, expect 
mostly clear skies and cool conditions with lows in the upper 
30s/low 40s.

Wednesday through Monday...

The upper-level pattern begins to shift rather drastically on 
Wednesday as phasing between the polar and subtropical jets begins to 
take place. In addition, a shortwave trough over the northern Plains 
moves southeastward towards the Ohio Valley. The combination of 
these factors, as well as remnant shortwave energy from the wave 
discussed from Tuesday will result in surface-based cyclogenesis 
that will produce a robust low pressure system. While ensemble 
members are in agreement on this taking shape, the main 
disagreements seen in LREF cluster analysis continues to be the 
progression, placement, and timing of these features 
phasing/developing with each other. 

For early Wednesday, conditions will be mild and dry, with 
increasing cloud cover as the day progresses. Decent southwesterly 
flow ahead cold front will allow temperatures to be in the mid to 
upper 60s by the afternoon. In addition, the southerly flow will 
allow for some moisture return to occur, with a narrow swath of 0.7-
0.9" PW (80th percentile climatologically) ahead of the front. Te 
front will begin to swing through the area late Wednesday into 
Wednesday night, resulting in our next chance for precipitation. 
LREF guidance does show a narrow area of 200-300 J/kg of SBCAPE 
overlapping with the area of higher moisture, and with deep layer 
shear of 30-40 kt as well as supportive upper-level dynamics, a few 
thunderstorms could also develop as the front swings through. The 
SPS does place most of the CWA under a wind-driven marginal risk for 
severe weather, the combination of the timing (late 
afternoon/evening into the overnight) and weak lapse rates aloft 
will cause this to be a very low-end threat. Given the fast 
progression of the front, currently expected to depart to the east 
by Thursday morning, accumulation totals will be rather limited, 
with less than 0.25" of QPF currently forecast.

A rather cold air mass will fill in over the area behind the front, 
along with surface high pressure building in. The combination of 
cold air advection and a decent pressure gradient overhead will make 
for a rather blustery Thursday. The most recent LREF has 10-15 mph 
sustained winds, along with 25-30 mph wind gusts lasting through 
Thursday evening. Temperatures are currently forecast in the upper 
40s to low 50s, but if enough cloud cover sticks around, many places 
could struggle to get above the 50 degree mark. The cold air mass 
will continue to be reinforced over the region through the start of 
the weekend thanks to multiple embedded shortwaves from an upper-
level low over the eastern Great Lakes region and southern Ontario 
passes overhead. While most places will be dry Thursday morning 
onwards, if enough post-frontal moisture does stick around, 
temperatures will be cold enough late Thursday night into Friday 
morning to allow for a few snowflakes to occur, especially in the 
eastern half of the CWA. Temperatures Friday and Saturday will 
struggle to get above 50 during the daytime, slightly warming on 
Sunday and Monday. Overnight lows will get quite chilly, with below-
freezing morning temperatures expected Friday through Monday. For 
the end of the forecast period on Monday, guidance has begun to pick 
up on a weaker shortwave passing through the region that could 
produce our next round of precipitation, but wide spread in the 
members keeps confidence low in any particular outcome at this time.
